chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
title: Replacing Willie Lewis in Benny Carter's band after Henderson
summary: Tired of the road with Henderson, Collins visited Kelly's Stables, heard Nat Cole and Benny Carter, and accepted Carter's offer to stay.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Are we back? Good. Speaking of Dizzy, I was working with Benny Carter at the Three Deuces, and he needed a trumpet player and I recommended Dizzy. I don't think Benny was really aware of Dizzy, but any way he hired Dizzy and the band was just tremendous. How I started working with Benny, at -- I think it was Kelly's Stables. I had been working, as I told you, with Fletcher Henderson, and man, we had been on the road, I'd been to Tupelo below Mississippi to two above Mississippi, two aside Mississippi. I was just so sick of Mississippi and all of the places. And we came back to Chicago, we had about a five day layoff, and I decided to go to New York, for the five days.

And I went to New York, and Nat Cole -- I hadn't seen Nat in years because when I went to New York he went to California so I didn't see him, but I had heard about what he was doing. But any way this was -- now, this had to be in 1941, around 1941, so at the Kelly's Stables Nat Cole was appearing, and also Benny Carter's band. So I went in and I heard Nat's group, and it was just beautiful. I just loved it, you know, and it -- I was also glad to see him, and surprised to hear him sing, you know, because Nat and I had vied for jobs around Chicago, these little gigs, and he was --

Nat was a tremendous pianist, he was a genius on this piano. But I never knew that Nat could sing, you know. When I heard him sing it was just something, and I would -- and Benny's band was good, and it was just good to get out of Mississippi. And Benny had a guitarist with him, a very good guitarist from Cleveland by the name of Willie Lewis. He was blues oriented. That was his background.

But any way, they had some argument or something, and I don't know whether Benny fired him that night or he quit, but any way Benny asked me to come with the band. So I got on the phone and called Fletcher in Chicago and told Fletcher that I wanted to stay, and Fletcher begged me to come back and I'd say Fletcher, you just can't do this to me, I'm so tired of the road and so and so and so and so. But if you insist. He said, well, John, if you just want to stay there, okay.
